ta-l1d31q2-d1e97.summary: The Prooemium of the second question of Distinction 31 announces two topics on Hilary's appropriation: its reason, and Augustine's remark that the image is equalled to what it images and not conversely, raising whether equality in God is mutual, which was settled in Dist. 19.

ta-l1d31q2-d1e109.summary: First argument that Hilary's appropriation is unfitting. Augustine says appropriations are made to exclude error, so power is attributed to the Father lest he be thought weak like aged fathers among us. But no one erred about the Father's eternity, as Arius did about the Son's, so eternity should rather be appropriated to the Son.
claims: Appropriations exclude error; eternity was denied of the Son.

ta-l1d31q2-d1e112.summary: Second argument. No likeness is found among equivocals, and eternity denies a principle of duration while innascibility denies a principle of origin, so eternity should not be appropriated to the Father by reason of his innascibility.
claims: 'Principle' in eternity and innascibility is equivocal.

ta-l1d31q2-d1e115.summary: Third argument, against the reply that eternity signifies the essence principally and innascibility consequently. When a notional term is added to an essential one, the whole cannot be predicated of a person lacking that notion, as 'begotten God' is not said of the Father, so if eternity included innascibility it would not fit the Son, which is Arian impiety.
claims: Including innascibility would deny eternity to the Son.

ta-l1d31q2-d1e119.summary: Fourth argument. According to Dionysius the beautiful and the good go together, all things desire both, and their Greek names are close; goodness is appropriated to the Spirit, not the Son, so beauty (species) should be too.

ta-l1d31q2-d1e122.summary: Fifth argument. To use is to refer something to obtaining what is to be enjoyed, and the Spirit is himself enjoyable and not referred to another end, so use should not be appropriated to him.
claims: Use refers to an end beyond.

ta-l1d31q2-d1e125.summary: Thomas's determination. Hilary's appropriation names three propers (Father, Image, Gift) and three appropriations: eternity in the Father, species (beauty) in the Image, the Son, and use in the Gift, the Spirit. Eternity includes being the principle of all duration as first measure, from which aevum and time flow, which resembles the Father's properties as principle by generation and spiration, paternity and common spiration; and it includes lack of principle, resembling his innascibility. Beauty, according to Dionysius, requires consonance and clarity, as people are beautiful with proportioned limbs and bright colour, and the Philosopher adds magnitude, since small people are well proportioned but not beautiful. These fit the Son's propers: as perfect image he has perfect consonance, equal and like without unlikeness; as true Son he has the Father's perfect nature and so magnitude, the perfection of divine nature (Dist. 19); as perfect Word he has the clarity that shines on all things, in which all things are resplendent. Augustine's words can also be read entirely by threefold consonance: of the Son with the Father, first equality; of the Son with himself, since all attributes in him are one, being and living the same; and with created things, whose ideas are one in him as he is one with the Father. Use includes being taken into the power of the will, fitting the Spirit as love (Augustine: that love, delight, happiness, or beatitude is the Spirit in the Trinity), and being ordered to another, fitting the Spirit, whose love overflows into all creatures as Gift.
claims: Eternity is appropriated to the Father as principle of duration without principle.
Beauty, as consonance, magnitude, and clarity, is appropriated to the Son as Image, Son, and Word.
Use, as taking into the will and ordering to another, is appropriated to the Spirit as Love and Gift.

ta-l1d31q2-d1e147.summary: Reply to the first argument. There is one principal reason for appropriation, likeness to the proper, but many consequent uses, one of which Augustine mentions, so nothing should be appropriated without the principal reason.
claims: Likeness to the proper is the principal reason for appropriation.

ta-l1d31q2-d1e150.summary: Reply to the second argument. Among chance equivocals like 'dog' there is no likeness, but among those said with respect to one principle there is a likeness of analogy or proportion, and 'principle' is of this kind, which is why the Philosopher reduces all such to one first principle.
claims: 'Principle' is analogical, not a chance equivocal.

ta-l1d31q2-d1e153.summary: Reply to the third argument: the argument does not hold.

ta-l1d31q2-d1e157.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. Beauty is desirable only as it takes on the character of good, as the true is also desirable, but by its proper character it has clarity and the features described, which resemble the Son's propers.
claims: Beauty is desirable only as good; by its own character it is clarity and proportion.

ta-l1d31q2-d1e160.summary: Reply to the fifth argument. 'Use' is taken in two ways (Dist. 1): commonly, as taking something into the power of the will, and strictly, as referring to an end. Here it is taken the first way, which includes enjoyment, so happiness or beatitude belongs to use. It also fits as including an order not to an end but to an effect, in which divine goodness is poured out most abundantly through the Spirit.
claims: Here 'use' is taken broadly, including enjoyment.

ta-l1d31q2-Dd1e92.summary: The Prooemium announces the reason for Hilary's appropriation and notes that the mutuality of equality was treated in Dist. 19.

ta-l1d31q2-Dd1e101.summary: Article 1 defends Hilary's appropriation. Eternity is appropriated to the Father as principle of all duration and without principle, resembling paternity, common spiration, and innascibility. Beauty, consisting in consonance, magnitude, and clarity, is appropriated to the Son as perfect Image, true Son, and Word. Use, as taking into the will and ordering to another, is appropriated to the Spirit as Love and Gift. Likeness to the proper is the principal reason for appropriation, 'principle' is analogical, and 'use' is taken broadly to include enjoyment.
claims: Eternity, beauty, and use are appropriated to Father, Son, and Spirit by likeness to their propers.

ta-l1d31q2.summary: Quaestio 2 of Book I, Distinction 31 explains Hilary's appropriation of eternity to the Father, beauty to the Son, and use to the Spirit. Each rests on likeness to the person's proper: eternity as principle without principle, beauty as the consonance, magnitude, and clarity of the perfect Image, Son, and Word, and use as the will's love overflowing as Gift.
claims: Hilary's appropriations rest on likeness to the persons' propers.
Beauty consists in consonance, magnitude, and clarity.
